text: Cassini wasn't trying to end the mission by choice, it was out of fuel for a stable orbit. The real reason for the final plunge is protecting Enceladus, the moon whose subsurface ocean makes it the top candidate for life at Saturn. If the spacecraft could linger in a loose trajectory, the craft or debris could one day intersect that moon and leave Earth microbes behind. A controlled crash into the gas giant's atmosphere is the cleanest way to keep that risk down, and it also got us one last flyby. Better safe than sorry when you're working around a possibly living moon.

I think the label is about ancestry, not where you happen to live. "Afro-American" doesn't claim that most Black Americans are currently from Africa. It signals descent from people who were brought from Africa, often through the slave trade, and the cultural history that came with them. That connection is real even if their families have been in the US for generations and no one has stepped foot on an African continent for a long time.

You'll also find "African American" used more formally, but the shorter form is a casual cultural label, not a literal geographic description. I'd also push back a bit on treating "black people" as one block. There's a lot of variation, and not every Black American traces a clear line to a single African country. The term works as an identifier for African descent in the US, not as a passport stamp. The question assumes current nationality, but the word is about descent, not origin by birthplace. It's a loose cultural tag, not proof of each person's exact family line.

The name is a historical marker. Most Black Americans aren't "from Africa" in the everyday sense, but the prefix points to where the ancestral roots lie. That's enough to explain the naming.

I'm glad you reached out. House buying has enough unknowns that it's easy to feel a bit lost. My take is to keep the basics straight first: what you can actually afford, what the area is really like at different times of day and on weekends, and what condition the place is in. Don't let excitement push you into a price point that's too high.

For the budget, start with the mortgage amount you can comfortably pay, then leave room for taxes, insurance, repairs and the odd emergency. A lot of people only count the monthly payment and then get surprised. The house itself matters too. Older places often cost less to buy but can be pricey to maintain. A nice neighborhood sounds great in a brochure, but check parking, noise, schools, and how the street feels when it's busy.

Before signing, get an independent inspection and read the contract's fine print. Seller disclosures only tell you what they chose to mention. If the offer is accepted, make sure your financing falls through if you can't get the loan, and that your deposit is protected.

I'd be happy to go over the actual questions one at a time.

Best,
Sam

It's not that inbreeding directly lowers IQ. What it does is raise the odds that two copies of the same gene end up together in the offspring. A lot of small effects on intelligence are spread through the genome, and when relatives mate, their children inherit more identical-by-descent genes. That exposes recessive alleles that would usually stay hidden in the general population.

The dip isn't a fixed amount for every child. It's cumulative, across many traits, and it interacts with environment too. In practice, the average for inbred families comes out a little below population norms, mostly because the hidden recessive load gets expressed more often. The scale is usually modest. The closer the relatives, the larger the expected drop, all else being equal. You can think of it as a quality-control problem rather than a specific defect.

The arm is not some special pain-free zone. What's going on is that pain isn't evenly spread across the body, and the upper arm has fewer pain-sensitive structures than the hands or feet, which are full of them. Muscle and bone can take the hit and spread force around, so a blow to the arm may feel duller than the same blow to a more exposed spot. Injury also triggers adrenaline and shock, which can blunt pain for a while, so it may seem less serious than it is. If the arm is injured near a joint or tendon, that spot hurts more, so location matters. A lot of it is perception, not physics: the brain compares what happens with what it expects, and the body can downplay pain while under stress. This does not mean the injury is minor. It means the sensation may be misleading at first.

The brace isn't about making your body rigid. It's about deciding where the impact forces hit you, and keeping your organs from slamming into your ribs and spine.

When you tuck your chin to your chest and wrap your arms across your chest, you stop your head from snapping back and your arms from flailing into the windshield or the seat in front. The head is the most vulnerable part, so that motion is the first thing to control.

Bending your knees slightly and keeping your feet on the floor helps too, because a hard stop with locked knees transfers the force straight up your legs and into your pelvis. Keeping them bent lets your legs absorb some of the shock.

This position is what you'll do in a crash landing or an emergency stop on the ground, and it works for a hard taxiing incident just as much as for a crash. The seatbelt still does most of the heavy lifting; the brace just makes sure your body doesn't fight itself during the deceleration.

It's not dramatic, it's just physics: less relative motion between your internal organs and the frame, less injury. The crew will call it out, and you'll have practiced it in training.

Most pre-industrial firms didn't die because nobody knew them; the business world changed too fast for them to keep going. A medieval guild, a trading house, or a monastic brewery could outlast generations, but once factories, railways and mass production arrived, the old ways lost ground quickly. Companies that stayed alive usually changed their name, ownership, or product so thoroughly that the original identity was gone. The interesting bit is that some old names do survive, but often in a form so different that they're hard to trace back. It's more like reinvention than disappearance. It's not a mystery, just a long stretch of change.

The bank is not cheaper because of the interest rate. Dealerships get a slice of the financing fee, and that fee gets hidden in the rate or charged separately. The bank doesn't pay anyone else, so it can quote a lower rate without the dealer's cut. That's the real reason.

You can test this yourself. Ask the dealer for the rate on paper and ask the bank for its rate on paper. The dealer's number will usually look lower, but once you add the dealer's financing fee, the bank's offer often wins. The fee can be a fixed amount or a percentage, and either way it lands on you.

Dealerships make money on financing, and that's part of the deal. They don't have to hand you the best possible rate if the fee covers the gap. Banks compete directly with each other, so their quotes are cleaner and more direct. There's no middleman taking a cut.

One practical thing: if you use the bank, make sure the car loan shows up under your name and the bank handles the title registration. It saves the headache of a dealer holding the title. I've seen buyers get burned when the dealer promised a low rate but buried the fee in a "doc fee" or "processing fee." Ask for the itemized breakdown, not just the headline rate.

The bank's total cost is usually lower because there's no dealer cut. That's the short version.

The patchwork of marijuana laws across US states is a real headache. You can legally buy a joint in one state and cross into the next where it is still a crime. State borders don't care that a patch of cannabis doesn't grow inside a zip code. I think the whole thing is ridiculous. People driving across state lines with a legal amount of weed in their glovebox are basically rolling the dice. A cop pulling you over doesn't care about your home state's rules once you hit that next state's pavement. You can be perfectly legal at home and technically a criminal on the road. The federal government still lists it on its controlled substances list, which makes the state laws even more confusing. I don't get why we treat a plant like it obeys imaginary lines drawn on a map. Here's the thing that always gets lost in the 'body as battery' picture. The heart's electrical system is the clearest example of what I mean. The sinoatrial node fires its own action potentials, and that's what pushes the whole heart through a beat, about sixty to a hundred times a minute. Those potentials are just sodium and potassium moving across cell membranes. The body doesn't generate current the way a power plant does. It moves charged particles around, and that movement is the whole electricity story. I keep coming back to that distinction.

Sampling older songs pulls a feeling out of an old recording and makes it do something new. I keep getting asked this because the legal side confuses people. The practical side is simpler than the paperwork.

The first move is to find the exact moment in an old record that still has teeth. I usually start with the original LP or CD, not the cleaned up streaming version. The scratch, room tone, and a little imperfection matter. In the DAW I cut the loop, time stretch it, tune it, and drop it under a new beat. The sample doesn't have to be a full phrase. A half second of a horn stab, a drum fill, or a voice saying one word can be the whole hook.

My head doesn't hurt because something inside is crushing the skull. That's what I kept believing, and it's not really right. A headache is mostly nerve pain. Irritated or stretched tissue sends pain signals up to the brain, and the brain reads that as pain on the outside of the head. The blood vessels can widen, and that changes the local pressure, which makes the nerves around them more sensitive.

I think that's why a mild headache feels like pressure, while a bad one feels like the skull is splitting. The vessels aren't squeezing me from the inside, they're part of the signal chain, not the whole story. That made me less afraid of getting one, because now I know a little more about what's actually happening up there.

I hit this buffet one Friday around 4:30 p.m., and to my surprise there wasn't a line to speak of. Two people walked out at $130, which honestly felt steep. Before going in I assumed the price would track a typical steakhouse, but after paying I realized the buffet actually came out a bit more expensive than I'd expected that steakhouse would be.

I was flat out disappointed there wasn't any steak on the menu. At that price I figured some kind of steak option would be there. What they did have was lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I've seen those same meats at other Las Vegas buffets for far less money, so they don't really justify the bill.

The seafood station carried Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. I've seen the Alaskan legs at plenty of Vegas buffets, but the rock crab claws were new to me and genuinely interesting. The catch was there were no crackers for the crab, and staff mentioned wooden mallets you could use, but our table sat so close to the one next to us that I didn't want to be cracking shells and sending bits over the border. So I just ate the legs and left the claws.

The Asian station didn't stand out much either; it reminded me a lot of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert was gelato and an assortment of pastries, nothing that really popped, and there were fresh juices, though I didn't try any.

On balance I'd call it acceptable but overpriced for what it serves. If you're curious it's worth one trip, especially with no wait, but if there's a long line I'd think twice.

The space bar rattles. It sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer, and the E key repeats now and then, so "example" turns into "eexample" and I backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it because of the switches. I asked the seller what they were and the answer took a week. By then I'd already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage, boxing it up, and being without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on my desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now. It still works for me, rattle and all.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. They never arrived because the sales rep recorded our delivery address incorrectly, mistaking her handwritten 7 for a 1. The intended address was 5407, but the package was sent to 5401. The residents of 5401 brought it to the local UPS store for return, and then it disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We didn't find out until several weeks later. While the dispute was still going, we placed an additional order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner stepped in and acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address, but said there'd be no refund until the shirts were returned. He even claimed we were partly responsible for not being friendly enough to the residents of 5401, four doors away. We ended up disputing the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got the credit.
